newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany set to loosen blood-based nationality law.
newsitem.headline: Germany set to loosen blood-based nationality law.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) were set to agree a plan on Monday which would for the first time concede the principle that German nationality is not only inherited, but can be acquired by being born in the country.

The CDU leadership was debating a proposal which would give dual nationality to immigrants' children born in Germany. At maturity, they would have to choose between German citizenship and that of their parents' country.

Germany is currently the only major Western industrial nation to maintain the principle, enshrined in an Imperial law dating back to 1913, that nationality is essentially passed down through the blood line.

But there is growing pressure from young members of Kohl's own party and from his liberal Free Democrat coalition partners to do more to integrate millions of immigrants and prevent them drifting away into ghettoes or turning to extremist groups.

"It has to be in our interests not to leave these young people out in the cold but to lead them to take on responsibilities towards Germany," said Horst Eylmann of the CDU, chairman of parliament's interior affairs committee.
"If I am born in Germany, go to school here, train for a job here...then I have automatically become German," he told North German Radio.
Even after 10 years of debate, the issue remains controversial within the coalition government.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther, a large number of CDU deputies and the arch-conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to the CDU, all oppose dual nationality.
Earlier this year Kanther imposed travel restrictions on children of immigrants from Turkey and north Africa.

"What difference does a passport make to the fact that a child of immigrants can feel foreign here because it has a different religion, skin of a different colour, speaks poor German or is treated badly by unpleasant contemporaries?" Kanther asked in an interview earlier this month.

Germany is home to some seven million foreigners, the bulk of them "guest workers" from Turkey, Yugoslavia and similar countries who began arriving in the 1960s to help fuel Germany's post-war economic miracle and are still a mainstay of the economy with 40,000 businesses of their own.

Around a quarter of them were born in Germany. They speak perfect German and feel Germany is their home, yet have the euphemistic status of "foreign co-citizens", excluded from the vote and from a large number of public sector jobs.
They can apply for naturalisation, but the procedure and qualifications are tough and under 50,000 people a year do so.
By contrast, more than 1.5 million ethnic Germans who have come here from eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union in the last eight years face no such restrictions.

Implicit in the opposition to dual nationality is the fear that Germany will become an even greater target for the refugees and asylum seekers who already come in their hundreds of thousands each year.

As a concession to CDU hardliners and the CSU, the proposal being debated on Monday ignores FDP demands that Germany should abandon the myth that it is not a "country of immigration" and instead select its own immigrants via fixed quotas.
